name: Bugatti Type 57SC Atlantic
hook: Bugatti built four Atlantics, and Jean Bugatti's own black one vanished around the outbreak of the Second World War and has never been found.
story: Molsheim, Alsace. Jean Bugatti keeps the second Atlantic for himself and has it finished in black. He designed the car. He drives it like a rolling business card: to shows, to customers, out on the roads around his father's factory. Then the war comes to the Rhine. The works evacuates south, and the black car, the story goes, is loaded up and sent toward Bordeaux. That is the last of it. No owner ever registered it. No confirmed photograph of it exists after 1938. Jean was killed in August 1939, aged thirty, testing a car on a closed road near the factory when he swerved around a cyclist. The one man who knew where it had gone was gone himself before anyone thought to ask. Of the four Atlantics, two survive untouched. A third was rebuilt after its owner died on a level crossing. The black one is simply missing, somewhere, and people are still looking for it.
description: The Type 57 SC Atlantic is a two-seat coupé built by Bugatti at Molsheim in eastern France between 1936 and 1938. Jean Bugatti, son of the founder Ettore, drew the body: a teardrop split by a riveted seam running nose to tail. That seam came from a magnesium-alloy show car whose panels were too flammable to weld, so they were riveted like an aeroplane. Underneath sits a supercharged twin-cam straight-eight of 3,257 cc. Four were built.
